ocean-warming-s1.title: Dissolved oxygen that seawater can hold at each temperature

table.caption: Most oxygen full seawater can hold at each temperature, mg/L (invented data for practice, close to measured values)

items.q: What is thermal expansion of seawater?
options: Water takes up more space as it warms
Water gains mass as it absorbs CO₂
Ice on land slides into the sea
Warm water rises and cold water sinks

why.correct: Thermal expansion: the same mass of water fills a larger volume when it is warmer. It is one of the two main causes of sea level rise.
options: Right: warmer water molecules move faster and spread apart, so the same mass fills more volume.
Dissolved CO₂ adds little volume; thermal expansion is caused by heat.
That is land ice adding water, a separate cause of sea level rise.
That describes circulation, not expansion.

items.q: Which two processes cause most of today’s sea level rise?
options: Melting sea ice and more rainfall
Melting land ice and thermal expansion
Dissolved CO₂ and melting sea ice
More rivers and sinking icebergs

why.correct: Land ice adds water; thermal expansion makes the existing water take up more room.
options: Sea ice already floats; rain is part of the water cycle and does not add new water.
Right: water from glaciers and ice sheets, plus warmer water expanding.
Neither raises sea level much.
Rivers return water that came from the ocean; they do not add new water.

items.q: Why does a warmer ocean hold less dissolved oxygen?
options: Warm water has more algae that eat the oxygen
Warm water is denser, squeezing oxygen out
Gases dissolve less in warm water
Fish breathe less in warm water

why.correct: Lower solubility plus a warm surface layer that mixes less both lower the oxygen in parts of the ocean.
options: The main reason is solubility; algae make oxygen by photosynthesis.
Warm water is less dense, not more.
Right: oxygen is less soluble as water warms, like a soda going flat faster when warm.
Fish need more oxygen in warm water, which makes the drop worse.

items.q: Describe the relationship in the data.
options: As temperature rises, oxygen rises
Oxygen stays about the same across temperatures
Oxygen rises up to 15 °C, then falls
As temperature rises, oxygen falls

why.correct: An inverse relationship: warmer seawater holds less oxygen.
options: The oxygen values fall as temperature goes up.
Oxygen changes by 5 mg/L across the table.
Oxygen falls the whole way.
Right: from 11.2 mg/L at 0 °C to 6.2 mg/L at 30 °C.

items.q: By what percent does the oxygen the seawater can hold change as it warms from 10 °C to 20 °C?

mistakes.why: You divided by the new value or reversed the order. Use (new − old) ÷ old × 100: (7.4 − 9.0) ÷ 9.0 × 100.
−1.6 mg/L is the change in oxygen, not the percent change. Divide by 9.0 and multiply by 100.

items.q: A cod population needs at least 7 mg/L of dissolved oxygen. Using the table, above about what temperature would full seawater fall below this level?
options: About 12 °C
About 22 °C
About 30 °C
About 2 °C

why.correct: Find where the values cross 7 mg/L: between 20 °C (7.4) and 25 °C (6.8).
options: At 15 °C the water still holds 8.1 mg/L.
Right: 7.4 mg/L at 20 °C and 6.8 mg/L at 25 °C, so it falls below 7 between them.
At 30 °C it is already 6.2 mg/L, well below 7.
Cold water holds the most oxygen, over 10 mg/L.

items.q: Explain how ocean warming could lower fish populations, using the data.

why.correct: Use the numbers, then link each step: warmer water, less oxygen, stressed fish, fewer fish.

specific.frame: As the ocean warms, dissolved oxygen ___, so fish ___, and populations ___.

o2.label: Oxygen
options: decreases
increases

why.1: The data show oxygen falling as temperature rises.

fish.label: Fish
options: struggle to get enough oxygen and move or die
grow faster with the extra oxygen
stop needing oxygen

why.1: There is less oxygen, not more.
why.2: Fish need oxygen at all temperatures, more in warm water.

pop.label: Populations
options: decrease
increase

why.1: Less oxygen and more stress reduce survival.

specific.model: As the ocean warms, dissolved oxygen decreases, from 9.0 mg/L at 10 °C to 7.4 mg/L at 20 °C, so fish struggle to get enough oxygen and move away or die, and local populations decrease because their bodies need more oxygen in warm water.

items.q: According to the figure, what share of the extra heat trapped since 1970 has the ocean taken up?
options: About 10%
About 50%
Less than 1%
About 90%

why.correct: Water can store far more heat than air, so most extra energy goes into the ocean.
options: That is far too small; the ocean takes most of the heat.
The figure says about 90%.
The ocean has absorbed most of it, about 90%.
Right: the ocean has absorbed about 90% of the extra heat.

items.q: Which effect in the figure raises sea level?
options: Water expands
Less dissolved oxygen
Coral bleaching
Species move

why.correct: Thermal expansion, together with melting land ice, raises sea level.
options: Right: thermal expansion makes the ocean take up more space.
Oxygen loss harms life but does not change sea level.
Bleaching harms reefs but does not change sea level.
Shifting ranges do not change sea level.

items.q: The figure shows less mixing in a warmer ocean. Why could this lower productivity at the surface?
options: The surface gets too dark for photosynthesis
Fewer nutrients rise from deep water
Warm water has too many nutrients
Phytoplankton sink into the warm layer

why.correct: A warm, light surface layer floats on cold, dense water, which blocks mixing that brings nutrients up.
options: Warming does not darken the surface layer.
Right: phytoplankton at the surface depend on nutrients mixed up from below.
The problem is fewer nutrients reaching the surface.
Phytoplankton stay near the surface; nutrients are what is missing.

items.q: Why does warmer water cause coral bleaching?
options: Warm water dissolves coral skeletons
Warm water carries more sunlight to the reef
Heat-stressed corals expel the algae that feed them
Warm water has more sea ice

why.correct: Corals live with algae in their tissues that make food by photosynthesis; heat stress breaks this mutualism.
options: Heat stress drives bleaching through the loss of algae.
The issue is heat stress, not more light.
Right: without their algae, corals lose color and much of their food.
Warm water has less sea ice, and reefs are in the tropics.

items.q: What drives the thermohaline circulation that moves water through the deep ocean?
options: The pull of the Moon on deep water
Wind blowing on the deep ocean floor
Heat rising from undersea volcanoes
Differences in temperature and salinity

why.correct: Cold, salty water near the poles is dense and sinks, driving a slow global loop of deep currents.
options: The Moon causes tides, not the deep conveyor belt.
Wind drives surface currents; deep circulation is driven by density.
Volcanic heat is not what drives the global conveyor belt.
Right: "thermo" is heat and "haline" is salt; both set water density.

items.q: How could melting Greenland ice slow the thermohaline circulation?
options: Fresh meltwater makes surface water less dense
Meltwater makes surface water saltier and heavier
Melting ice cools the whole ocean to freezing
Meltwater adds more dissolved oxygen

why.correct: The circulation depends on dense water sinking in the North Atlantic; fresher, warmer water there sinks less.
options: Right: less salty water sinks less readily, weakening the sinking that drives the loop.
Meltwater is fresh, so it lowers salinity.
The meltwater cools a region a little; the key change is lower salinity.
Oxygen does not drive the circulation.

items.q: Which are effects of ocean warming? Select all that apply.
options: Coral bleaching on tropical reefs
Fish moving toward the poles
More dissolved oxygen in surface water
A thicker stratospheric ozone layer

why.correct: Warming bleaches corals, lowers oxygen, shifts species and raises sea level.
options: Right: heat stress drives bleaching.
Right: many species move to stay in their range of tolerance.
Warm water holds less oxygen, not more.
Ocean warming does not change ozone.

items.q: The average temperature of a sea’s surface rose by 0.9 °C over 60 years. Write the setup for the average rate of warming in °C per decade, then the answer.

mistakes.why: That is the rate per year. A decade is 10 years, so 60 years is 6 decades: 0.9 ÷ 6.
Divide the change by the number of decades, do not multiply.
0.015 °C per year is the rate per year. Multiply by 10 for per decade, or divide 0.9 by 6 decades.
